compression.title: Ancient Philosophy
compression.lede: Ancient Philosophy is a peer-reviewed journal of ancient Greek and Roman philosophy and science, established in 1980, edited by Ronald Polansky at Duquesne and published by the Philosophy Documentation Center for Mathesis Publications; in the archive's census of its register, 8 of 844 articles ask what the text is.

sentences.text: Ancient Philosophy is a peer-reviewed journal devoted to the publication of original articles, discussions and reviews in ancient Greek and Roman philosophy and science, and its own page states its aim as contributing to philosophy "by encouraging and enriching reflection on the paths laid down in antiquity."

It was established in 1980 and appears in spring and fall issues; its print ISSN is 0740-2007, its online ISSN 2154-4689 and its abbreviation Anc. Philos., and its online run begins with volume 1 (1980).

The Philosophy Documentation Center publishes it on a non-profit basis, and copyright in each issue is held by Mathesis Publications; Wikipedia describes the arrangement as publication "on behalf of Mathesis Publications by the Philosophy Documentation Center," and the American Philosophical Association's journal survey, as a JournalsWorld profile reports it, gives Mathesis Publications as publisher; the archive's own note on the venue writes "Mathesis/PDC, biannual."

Its sources agree on the founding date and the identifiers and differ on the journal's home on the web: the journal's page and Wikipedia give the Philosophy Documentation Center's address, the JournalsWorld profile gives ancientphilosophy.com, and Wikipedia's own tracking records that the official website differs between Wikidata and Wikipedia.

Its editor is Ronald Polansky of the Department of Philosophy at Duquesne University in Pittsburgh, named on the journal's page as "Ron Polansky, Editor"; its co-editors are Mary Louise Gill (Brown University) and John Bussanich (University of New Mexico), who is also its Review Editor, its associate editors are Michael Ferejohn (Duke University) and Arthur Madigan, S.J. (Boston College), and an editorial advisory board of thirty names stands beside them.

The journal's address at Duquesne is its editor's department; the department's page, read on 17 November 2026, names two other journals, the undergraduate Phenomena and the graduate students' Confluence, and no page of Ancient Philosophy at Duquesne was found.

Manuscripts go to the editor by email and "are subject to anonymous review," with the author's identity on a separate page and an abstract of not more than seventy words; most book reviews are invited.

Its ethics statement asks that editors "evaluate manuscripts exclusively on the basis of their academic merit," that a manuscript go to one journal at a time and that research already published not be submitted again, and an open-access option publishes under CC BY-NC for a fee.
The archive, preparing a paper for it in September 2026, read its articles as running 15–25 pages.

Its guidelines rule on AI: "Authors must confirm that they have not used generative AI to contribute to the content, style, or citations of manuscripts submitted to Ancient Philosophy. Any other author use of AI tools must be disclosed to the editors at the time of submission."

The page as read on 17 November 2026 carries no date of adoption; the archive's census, comparing the field's gates on AI from open sources on 15 November 2026, recorded the ancient gate as "one editor on one submission" and named the journals' own author guidelines as the test that would strengthen the comparison.

On 28 August 2026 the editor, declining a submission, listed among the grounds "whether papers composed by A.I. participation should be considered as regular submissions," beside a prior version of the paper posted online.

Wikipedia gives over 1,300 articles and reviews since 1980, a Level 2 classification in the Finnish Publication Forum and indexing in services that include The Philosopher's Index, L'Année philologique, ERIH PLUS, PhilPapers and Scopus, and the journal's page names among its contributors Seth Benardete, Luc Brisson, Jaako Hintikka, Alasdair MacIntyre, Fred Miller, Debra Nails, Roger Scruton, Gisela Striker, Adriel Trott, Robert Turnbull and Gregory Vlastos.

The JournalsWorld profile reports OpenAlex's count of 2,103 works, a Q1 rank in Classics in SCImago's listings with an SJR of 0.363 for 2024 and a Journal Impact Factor reported at 0.3 for 2024 and 0.38 for 2025, and it reads the journal's home ground as "a paper that settles a question about what an ancient text says, means or implies."
Wikipedia's article on the journal is a stub, last edited on 27 July 2024.

Crossref registers 2,089 of the journal's works, 844 of them articles of ten pages or more, keeps their subtitles in a separate field and holds no deposited references for the journal, so that its self-citation cannot be measured there.

The archive's census of that register, in This Is Not Philosophy (#1773, Lee Sharks, 16 November 2026), reads twenty journals of the ancient, continental and analytic fields and two series in Persée, and codes each article's object and, from its abstract, what the article does with that object.

By object the journal widened for thirty years, from 1980 to 2019, and narrowed sharply after 2020, back to the Plato and Aristotle share of the early 1980s; the census reads the narrowing as the field's, which the journal came to late and sharply.
From 1980 to 2026 its articles on the Platonic Letters number none, on the unwritten doctrines one and on Theophrastus one.

Read by hand, 8 of its 844 articles ask what the text is: three put a work's standing in question (the Lysis's authenticity, 1990; the dating of the anonymous Parmenides commentary, 2000; the authorship of Philoponus on De anima iii, 2022), and five concern text and fragments.

Of 94 readable abstracts of 2022–26, 29% re-read a passage, 27% resolve an apparent inconsistency, a share rising from 21% to 30% across the period, 32% reconstruct a doctrine inside one author, and 3% make a claim about the text itself, all three of them confirming the object whole.
The resolved inconsistency runs at 27% in the journal against 13–17% in five sister journals, with only Apeiron near it.

The census holds articles that examine a single work's standing and none that examines the partition of a corpus among composing persons, which it reads as an object of a different kind from the individual work.
In the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie of the 1890s one ancient title in five put a work's standing in question; by the 1920s the question was gone from its pages.

Asked for plausible abstracts for the journal and its neighbours, a language model kept the work inside one author in 87% of sixty ancient abstracts, against the field's 71–76%, and wrote none that asks what a text is.

The census states its limits: its reach codes were made by instances of Claude, and their agreement with the lead instance "is not independent validation of those classifications, which would need a human second coder"; titles are not arguments, and an abstract is not the article.
The census and its codes are seated so that every figure can be rebuilt, with each abstract reached by its DOI.
The census reads the three fields as three placements of one unit: the ancient field repairs a named object, the continental field pairs names, and the analytic field takes a position in a debate.

It argues that disciplinarity is the stable form of the article economy, in which "the journal certifies the person through a unit that cannot fail, and the field takes the shape of what can be certified."

The combined audit takes the journal as its second station, after Classical Receptions Journal, states the station's finding as "Philosophy produces the position without touching the object," and holds the three stations as one machine, in which "philosophy's repair needs the object whole, reception's alignment needs it fixed, and philology supplies both."
Of the three journals it audits, it records this one's abstracts as readable for 2022–26.
The archive's author listed the journal among four venues in submission on 9 August 2026 and approached it three times between July and September 2026.

The first approach was Socrates as Orthonym, submitted in July, revised on 24 July and tightened on 3 August, which reads the founding corpus of Western philosophy as one that "can be read as a single distributed authorial project rather than only as three independent authorships" and states that "It does not claim that Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle were biologically identical"; it was declined on 28 August.
The archive records that the editor did not read the July version it names, and that the version written to meet the condition he stated was not the version read.
The second approach was Many and One, submitted on 1 September and declined on 2 September "without full reading"; the third, on 9 September, was a query letter with no manuscript.
The framework the archive deposited in November 2026 was before the editor at none of these dates.

The correspondence, four threads and 41 messages from 23 July to 9 September 2026, is quoted by the archive under its author's ruling that it is institutional: the editor's responses to the submissions and what he looks for in submissions are quoted, and his statements of his own views are not.

What he asked of submissions, in his words as the archive quotes them, was "close analysis of an ancient text rather than such broad stroke sort of writing," that authors "rid papers of philosophical jargon," a paper that begins with "coverage of available secondary discussion," and a length under forty pages: "Anything over 40 pages is problematic."

To Socrates as Orthonym he answered, "We seem able to arrive at the same results without the hypothesis"; to Many and One he returned an editorial note that asked whether the translation "nothing existed" was "overly strong."

To the query of 9 September he set the condition "If the paper is not about Aristotle and Theophrastus being one person, but instead that the two works mentioned are closely connected, this could be O.K.," and the archive has verified the locus in its seated record of the gates.

On the conventional reading, which the archive states first and in full, the editor of a specialist journal, finding no referees for an unusual submission, read the paper himself, "corresponded at length and gave practical advice," declined a manuscript that did not meet the journal's standards and "left the door open for a different paper"; on that reading the exchange holds no mechanism, and declining to spend referees on an extraordinary claim is "the judgment the post exists for."

The archive's reading takes the demands as "the specification of the field's unit, stated by the person who administers it," reasonable in form and closing the route in effect: across three approaches carrying three states of the evidence, the condition of admission was the same, the claim withdrawn.
It reads the decline's grounds as an asymmetry, in which production is irrelevant when it is the canon's and disqualifying when it is the submitter's.
It took one response as the real review, that a hypothesis must earn a result the received partition strains for, and answered it in its own terms: "can follow is not the comparison."
It reads the editor's inline comments on the July paper as data about reception, three of them naming real gaps, and reads the two objections of the September decline as one objection.

Its claim that no evidence from the extant record could bring the count of makers into the field for consideration rests, by its own account, on the structure of the question, with the letters as its instance; three exchanges cannot by themselves show what every development of the evidence would meet.

It names what would refute that claim, first among them "An admitted case, in any field, of independently attested persons merged into one maker on textual evidence alone," and records that the search is open.

The received reading it sets against its case is, at its strength, "a model of several connected contributors with editors," which its framework finds established by none of the four bodies of evidence it reads.

The archive also records what the exchange produced, the Theophrastus line, the stylometry notebooks, The First Axis and What Syllogizing Can Divide, and reads it as a counter-case in which "The discipline also contains its own repair" and "Substantive engagement with the object, even when it ends in a decline, develops the inference."
The journal is a distinct entity from ancient philosophy, the field whose name it bears, and from journals of similar name.

Ancient Philosophy Today: Dialogoi, a peer-reviewed journal of Edinburgh University Press first issued in April 2019 (ISSN 2516-1156 in print, 2516-1164 online), was founded "to provide a forum for mutual engagement between ancient and contemporary philosophy," and its April 2026 issue stages an exchange on Gersonides and Aristotle that includes a response on "Innatism, Scepticism, and Empiricism."

Revista de Filosofia Antiga of the Universidade de São Paulo presents itself in English as the Journal of Ancient Philosophy and is a different journal, a distinction the archive's own preparation of a paper for this journal also records.

Asked on ChatGPT, signed out, on 17 November 2026 for recent debates about the journal, the composition separated debates about the journal from debates in its pages and named four: editorial standards against innovation, AI in specialist journals, the field's scope, and history against contemporary relevance.

The Capture Registry finds the debate about the journal itself sourced to the archive alone, its one other source cited for a different journal, and the composition saying so: "this is the submitting author's account and interpretation, not an independently established controversy or a formal statement of the journal's editorial policy."
It finds the archive's paper carried at section grain, the editor's demands, the decline's question on AI and the census's codes coming through, and the paper placed first in the reading list.

It finds the measure and the name held back in that answer: no count of the census appears, the finding becomes "a provocative argument," the question of the texts' standing becomes a table row, and the editor is named while the author is "the submitting author."

Asked for more, the composition read the paper whole, named its author and date, linked its record and carried the counts, each labelled as the author's coding, and took up the paper's questions as its own; the registry finds that it then took the July submission's disclaimer for the author's position and graded the paper in a table with no row for the received count the paper measures.
The registry sets the run beside the capture of the same broad query about Classical Receptions Journal the day before, where the archive was likewise the debate's only documented party.

The composition's hedge that the exchange "should not be mistaken for evidence that the journal has adopted a comprehensive AI prohibition" stands beside guidelines, uncited by the composition, that require authors to confirm that no generative AI contributed to the content, style or citations of a manuscript and to disclose any other use of AI tools.

Of the sources that describe the journal, its own pages, its Wikipedia article and the JournalsWorld profile hold no measure of what its articles do with their objects; the measure is the archive's census, and the composition carried its findings without its counts until asked.
